morning.title: Where Are The Aircraft Carriers?: October 17, 2026
morning.text:
With a flight deck packed with carrier-based aircraft, including stealthy fifth-generation F-35Cs, the USS Theodore Roosevelt pulled into Yokosuka, Japan, on Friday. Roosevelt is the first non-resident U.S. carrier to visit the key naval port, strategically located on the east side of Japan, in more than four years. Yokosuka is home to the USS George Washington and America’s only forward-based Carrier Strike Group (CSG).

The Roosevelt, which serves as the flagship of CSG 9, escorted by guided-missile cruiser USS Chosin and destroyer USS Decatur, completed the journey from San Diego in 19 days − maneuvering around a typhoon in the Western Pacific − and will participate in the upcoming combined exercise Keen Sword 27. Meanwhile, the USS George H.W. Bush departed Thailand after a five-day port call and returned to the Middle East, and the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived home after a nearly eleven-month combat deployment.

In This Article

  • Theodore Roosevelt Docks In Yokosuka, Japan; First Visiting Carrier In Four Years
  • Abraham Lincoln’s Homecoming
  • George H.W. Bush Leaves Thailand And Returns To The Middle East
  • F-35C Lightning II Operates from A Ford Class Carrier For The First Time
  • Big Deck Fleet At A Glance

Here’s TWZ’s weekly carrier tracker monitoring America’s flattop fleet, including deployed CSGs and Amphibious Ready Groups (ARGs), using publicly available open-source information. Check out last week’s report here.

Theodore Roosevelt Docks In Yokosuka, Japan; First Visiting Carrier In Four Years

Roosevelt and Chosin chopped into the U.S. 7th Fleet-Pacific Command (PACOM) area of responsibility (AOR) and arrived at Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka on the morning of October 16. The CSG will spend a few days in port before beginning participation in exercise Keen Sword, a “premier joint-bilateral field training exercise designed to increase readiness and interoperability between the Japan Self-Defense Forces and U.S. military forces,” according to the 7th Fleet press release. The brief visit allows the crew to complete maintenance, resupply, and disembark for liberty before resuming routine operations.

“Our crew is honored to visit Yokosuka and experience the rich culture and hospitality of Japan,” the commanding officer of Roosevelt, Capt. Will Mathis, said in the release. “Port visits like this are vital for crew morale and mission readiness, allowing our Sailors to rest, recharge, and prepare to operate seamlessly alongside our allies during exercise Keen Sword.”

The five-ship CSG, the composition of which a Navy official confirmed to TWZ, is currently operating on a disaggregated basis − a common practice employed by strike groups with multiple ongoing missions. The duo that departed the U.S. at the end of September linked up with another element of the group, Pearl Harbor-based guided missile destroyer USS Decatur, as they were steaming westbound past the Hawaiian Islands, based on public Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. Decatur arrived in Yokosuka the day after Roosevelt but was not mentioned in the press release.

USS Carl M. Levin, also stationed in Hawaii, was the first ship from the group to deploy, according to DVIDS, the military’s content-sharing platform. Levin departed on September 9 and is operating at an undisclosed location. USS Paul Hamilton, the final ship assigned to CSG 9 to deploy, left San Diego on October 10 after onloading ammo at Bravo Pier and moored at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam on October 15, AIS data shows. Henry J. Kaiser class fleet replenishment oiler USNS Tippecanoe supported the group’s transit across the Pacific, conducting multiple replenishments-at-sea (RAS), and recently entered the East Sea/Sea of Japan via the Tsugaru Strait before going dark on AIS.

Multiple reports indicated that medium unmanned surface vessel (MUSV) Seahawk (2) deployed with the group, which would represent a significant operational achievement and the first time a drone boat was assigned to a CSG, but the MUSV quietly slipped out of Point Loma on October 8, more than ten days after Roosevelt. Seahawk reappeared on AIS and docked in Hawaii for a couple days before continuing its journey westbound in the Pacific on October 16. If Seahawk is assigned to CSG 9, it is currently disaggregated, and whether it will join Roosevelt to participate in exercise Keen Sword 27 is unknown.

Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao seemingly confirmed the deployment, saying during a panel at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) convention that “the Teddy Roosevelt carrier strike group just deployed on October 8 with a medium sized unmanned surface vessel. This is the first carrier strike group to ever deploy with a large size unmanned surface vessel.” However, Roosevelt was more than halfway to Japan on the date referenced. “This is a force multiplier, imagine having more guns out there,” he added.

TWZ reached out to the Secretary’s office for clarification and to confirm the deployment but did not receive a response. “Seahawk’s operations represent continued progress in the Navy’s efforts to integrate unmanned systems into Fleet operations. As with any emerging capability, we continue to learn, adapt, and refine how these systems are employed,” a Navy official told us.

Abraham Lincoln’s Homecoming

Surrounded by small boats, with hundreds of spectators lining the channel in San Diego Bay and thousands more watching online, the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived home from a historic ten-and-a-half-month combat deployment. The flagship of CSG 3 and her crew of more than 5,000 Sailors and Marines served as the tip of the spear in the war against the Iranian regime, first during Operation Epic Fury and then the subsequent blockades, and set a new record for the most consecutive days at sea without a port call.

Lincoln pulled into Naval Air Station North Island and moored at Berth Lima on October 8, 321 days after casting off on November 21, 2025. Sailors in dress whites manned the rails as the carrier transited the bay, escorted on both sides by small boats and jet skis flying American flags, while family and friends eagerly waited pierside for their return. The video below, shared by the Pentagon, captures the moment.

Lincoln now lays claim to the second-longest deployment in the modern carrier era, falling just five days short of the 326-day post-Vietnam record held by the USS Gerald R. Ford. The flattop traveled over 93,000 nautical miles during the cruise − more than four trips around the Earth, a post by the public affairs officer highlighted − and conducted 72 replenishments-at-sea, received 20-plus million gallons of aviation fuel, and flew more than 14,000 sorties that totaled 28,500 flight hours, a press release from the Navy highlighted.

The release confirmed for the first time that Lincoln broke the previous record of 206 days set by USS Dwight D. Eisenhower during the COVID pandemic for days spent underway between port visits, as TWZ first reported. “The ship’s 208 uninterrupted days at sea between Guam and Oman, and its 286 consecutive days at sea between departing San Diego and arriving in Thailand, are record-breaking marks for modern aircraft carriers.”

Lincoln’s cruise took her through both U.S. 7th Fleet and U.S. 5th Fleet AORs. During Operation Epic Fury, which began on February 28 and lasted almost 40 days, Lincoln took up station in the northern Arabian Sea as Commander, Task Force (CTF) 50 and pressured Iran’s southern flank. When major combat operations wound down, the carrier and her air wing patrolled and enforced the blockade line during both rounds that followed.

Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 9, the “Navy’s premier next-generation air wing that served as the primary offensive power” for CSG 3, flew 14,037 sorties − including 4,000 combat missions − and dropped more than 1.37 million pounds of ordnance on thousands of targets while employing 1,499 precision weapons. “This concentrated firepower significantly degraded Iranian Navy capabilities,” a separate statement noted.

“The rapid mobilization and combat execution of CVW-9 during Operation Epic Fury demonstrated the unmatched flexibility of a U.S. Navy carrier strike group,” Capt. J.W. Stigi, commander of CVW-9, said in the statement. “Pairing fifth-generation F-35C stealth and sensor fusion with fourth-generation workhorse strike and electronic attack platforms, Team Shogun destroyed Iran’s conventional Navy and secured vital maritime chokepoints in support of our commander’s objectives.”

Kill marks painted on the island superstructure show CSG 3 destroyed 106 one-way attack drones fired by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), 34 Iranian Navy and IRGC ships, 23 inbound cruise missiles, and 10 enemy submarines. The strike group dropped 1,463 air-to-ground munitions in total, a Sailor explaining the marks said in a video on social media.

George H.W. Bush Leaves Thailand And Returns To The Middle East

The USS George H.W. Bush and her destroyer escort, USS Delbert D. Black, departed Phuket, Thailand, on October 9 after a five-day liberty visit. “Nearly 5,000 Sailors from across the strike group experienced the sights and sounds Thailand has to offer, deepening their understanding of the Thai people and strengthening interpersonal bonds,” according to a press release.

“The Sailors and I had an amazing time in this beautiful country, and I sincerely thank the people of Thailand for their incredible welcome,” Capt. Justin T. Issler, the commanding officer of George H.W. Bush, said about the stop. “This port visit to Phuket was a tremendous opportunity for the crew. We are grateful to our Thai allies for hosting us, and we look forward to continuing our mission here in 7th Fleet, alongside Thailand and our other regional allies and partners.”

Bush dropped anchor approximately two nautical miles south of Ao Makham Deep Sea Port on October 4 after 187 consecutive days at sea. After leaving Phuket, the carrier stopped broadcasting AIS while steaming due south at 10 knots. Imagery on DVIDS confirms that the CSG returned to the Middle East and operating in the U.S. 5th Fleet AOR to “support maritime security and stability,” joining the George Washington CSG once again as the second strike group in the region.

Destroyer USS Mason, which deployed as the integrated air and missile defense (IAMD) commander for the CSG but has disaggregated at times, arrived in Singapore on October 5, likely for a port call. The Arleigh Burke class destroyer departed on October 9 and was last tracked heading northwestbound in the Malacca Strait, likely to rejoin the CSG. The other two destroyers assigned to the CSG, USS Ross and USS Donald Cook, remained in 5th Fleet during the visit.

F-35C Lightning II Operates from A Ford Class Carrier For The First Time

Marking a major milestone, an F-35C Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter made the first arrested landing aboard a Gerald R. Ford class carrier, the Navy’s newest and most advanced class of aircraft carriers that are being built to replace the aging Nimitz fleet. The trap was made by Lt. Cmdr. Robert Mason with the “Salty Dogs” of Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23 aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy in the Western Atlantic on October 13. The first catapult launch followed the next day, pictures on DVIDS showed.

VX-23, based out of Naval Air Station Patuxent River in Maryland, is part of the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division and was putting Kennedy through the ongoing Aircraft Compatibility Testing to assess the “operational capabilities of the ship’s aircraft launch and recovery equipment.” A team from the Patuxent River-based F-35 Integrated Test Force, detached to the ship, conducted the evaluation using a specially instrumented example of the jet. One of the two pictured was externally equipped with an inert Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM) bomb.

The Navy took preliminary acceptance of Kennedy, which is still considered a Pre-Commissioning Unit, on September 29. This process allows the service to conduct at-sea testing and build underway proficiency while the shipbuilder, Huntington Ingalls Industries, completes final system checks ahead of expected delivery in spring 2027. Kennedy got underway on October 13 and returned to her homeport of Naval Station Norfolk three days later.

The lead ship of the class, the USS Gerald R. Ford, does not currently embark F-35Cs and will need upgrades to field the Navy’s most advanced jet. Back in 2019, TWZ warned that the stealth jet wouldn’t fly from the troubled class for years. Because of this, Congress required that Kennedy be equipped to embark F-35Cs, which led to additional delays for the Navy’s next carrier.

Big Deck Fleet At A Glance

Overall, three U.S. carriers are deployed, three are working up in various states of readiness, three are in maintenance availabilities, one is post-deployment, one is being used primarily for training before deactivation next year, and another will be delivered in 2027. Two amphibious ready groups are deployed, one is forward-deployed, three are working up or in port, and three are in maintenance.

Note: Positions are general approximations. Non-deployed LHA/LHD amphibious warships are not shown.

Contact the author: ian@twz.com or @ianellisjones

Mumbai to Host Italian Navy’s Multi-Purpose Combat Vessel
morning.text:
Italian Multi-Purpose Combat Ship (MPCS) Giovanni Delle Bande Nere will make a port call in Mumbai from October 18 to 22 as part of its operational deployment in the Indo-Pacific, the Italian Navy said on Friday.
In a press release issued by the Public Information and Communication Office of the Italian Navy General Staff, the Navy said the ship will be involved in naval diplomacy and international cooperation activities during the visit, and a representative of the Indian Navy will welcome her on arrival in port.
“ITS Giovanni Delle Bande Nere, which set sail on the 3rd of May from Taranto, will make ten port calls during the deployment, consolidating Italy’s presence in the region as part of wider international cooperation to showcase the ‘Italian System’ in technological, industrial and cultural terms, and promoting Italian excellence during the major events organised throughout the visits,” the press release stated.
The visit reaffirms the Italian Ministry of Defence’s commitment to demonstrating the nation’s capability to operate in global maritime contexts and to strengthening cooperation with partner navies, thereby promoting the protection of maritime communication lines and freedom of navigation, the Italian Navy added.
A presentation event dedicated to the Italian defence industry will be held on board the ship on October 21.
Last month, the Indian Navy’s sail training ship, INS Sudarshini, set sail from Livorno in Italy, after completion of a successful port call.
“The Indian Navy’s sail training ship, INS Sudarshini, set sail from Livorno, Italy, on September 12 on completion of a successful port call. During her stay, the ship participated in a series of professional interactions and cross-training visits, strengthening bonds of friendship and maritime partnership between the two nations,” India’s Ministry of Defence had said.
Admiral Giuseppe Berutti Bergotto, Chief of the Italian Navy, visited INS Sudarshini and interacted with the ship’s crew and trainees.
He was briefed on the ship’s voyage and training activities.
The engagement reflected the expanding maritime cooperation and longstanding friendship between India and Italy.
(IANS)

morning.title: RBA Signs MoU With Andhra Pradesh for Stratospheric Technology
morning.text:
In a new move towards near space technologies, Red Balloon Aerospace (RBA) hopes to open a new facility in Amaravati, Andhra Pradesh, to build new platforms for stratospheric infrastructure.
The company announced the plan while announcing its memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Andhra Pradesh Economic Development Board (APEDB). The agreement, RBA said, was “a stepping stone towards a partnership of the long haul” and the “attention and cooperation of the state government” had helped it progress its technology development programme.
RBA is developing near space infrastructure that will be able to fly at the altitudes of the stratosphere not reached by conventional aircraft and lower than the orbital environment. Service requirement such as communication, observation, monitoring etc. requiring persistent coverage over selected areas could be provided from platforms operating in this region.
The proposed Amaravati plant will be for the development of these next-generation platforms, the company said. It has applications in mobility, communications, financial services, geospatial governance, environmental and infrastructure monitoring and disaster response. But RBA has not yet revealed the amount of money the facility will cost, the capacity it plans to build, when the construction will be completed, or which platforms will be built at the facility.
The company also highlighted its Mission SANA programme as an example of how government support can help to speed up deep-tech development. The mission was successfully executed in less time than expected, due to timely authorisations, RBA said. The company did not disclose any other technical information about Mission SANA in the announcement, such as the platform for using it, its mission objectives or what impact it has had.
The pace at which experimental systems move towards operational deployment can be determined by regulatory approvals and access to testing infrastructure for companies developing emerging aerospace technologies. Specialized development and testing, such as testing in low-pressure environments and testing with temperature extremes and atmospheric wind and long flight operations may be needed for stratospheric platforms. Specifically the need depends on the design of the platform and its mission.
The proposed facility by RBA could help qualify the state of Andhra Pradesh to become a hub for the development of deep tech startups as well as provide the expertise of aerospace engineering to the local industry. INS Samarthak: 75% Indigenous Content in Newly Commissioned Warship
morning.text:
The multi-purpose warship INS Samarthak was commissioned into the Indian Navy at the Karwar-based Karwar Naval Base (Kadamaba Naval Base) on Friday, in a ceremony presided over by Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan.
Karnataka Labour and Employment Minister Santosh S. Lad attended the commissioning ceremony.
INS Samarthak is the first of four multi-purpose vessels being inducted into the Indian Navy. The commissioning was formally marked by hoisting the national tricolour bearing the Navy’s insignia aboard the warship, signalling its induction into service.
The warship has been designed to support future defence operations and incorporates a significant proportion of indigenous equipment. Around 75 per cent of the equipment used in the vessel is indigenously developed, while certain technologies have been sourced from abroad.
Senior naval officials attended the ceremony, including Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, Flag Officer Commanding-in-Chief of the Western Naval Command Vice-Admiral Sanjay Vatsayan, and head of the warship production division Vice-Admiral Sanjay Sadhu.
Rear Admiral Vikram Menon, Flag Officer Karnataka Naval Area, and Commander Sushil Singh, commanding officer of INS Samarthak, were also present.
Key representatives of Larsen & Toubro Ltd (L&T) and OEMs associated with indigenous equipment were also present during the commissioning ceremony.
Designed and constructed by L&T Shipyard, INS Samarthak marks a significant milestone in India’s indigenous shipbuilding journey as the first major warship to be built by an Indian private shipyard.
The commissioning is a powerful testament to the growing maturity and capability of the nation’s private shipbuilding industry and reflects the deepening synergy between the Indian Navy and the Indian shipbuilding industry in advancing the national vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat.
Conceived as a versatile platform for trials and evaluation, INS Samarthak embodies the enhanced technological and operational capabilities of the Indian Navy in the 21st century.
With over 75 per cent indigenous content, the Ship incorporates extensive modular construction and pre-outfitting, significantly optimising the build process and construction timelines.
The project has also contributed to employment generation, capability development and plough back into the Indian economy.
Aptly named Samarthak, meaning ‘The Proponent’, the ship represents the spirit of a dependable enabler, capable of supporting multiple missions and has been designed with inherent versatility and adaptability, enabling it to undertake a diverse range of operational and developmental tasks.
True to its name, INS Samarthak is capable of undertaking maritime surveillance and reconnaissance, offshore patrolling, and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief operations, as required.
The official statement said, “Addressing the gathering, the Chief Guest underscored the strategic significance of indigenously built naval platforms in strengthening the country’s maritime capabilities and enhancing the Indian Navy’s ability to undertake an increasingly wide spectrum of operational and testing missions.”
The commissioning of INS Samarthak reinforces the nation’s commitment to maritime security, regional stability and cooperative engagement across the Indian Ocean Region. The ship epitomises India’s sustained pursuit of a self-reliant and resilient domestic defence industrial ecosystem.
The induction of INS Samarthak significantly strengthens India’s ability to test and train on new sensors and weapons developed indigenously by domestic industry. The ship’s versatility is an advantage in an unpredictable maritime environment, given the rise of non-traditional maritime threats.
Source: IANS

morning.title: BSF Seeks 32 Combat Bulletproof Vehicles for Jammu and Kashmir
morning.text:
The BSF have issued a bid for 32 Light Bullet Proof Vehicles (LBPVs) in combat configuration for its J&K frontier. The procurement is being issued by the BSF Directorate General under the Ministry of Home Affairs and has a 90 day performance period with a bid submission date of 2nd November 2026.
The tender (published 12th October) is listed as ID 2026_BSF_930024_1 and Ref P-4/LBPV/BSF/2026/6779-80. It is a domestic purchase of goods under the title “Light Bullet Proof Vehicles – Combat Variant, Qty-32 Nos”. The process is being managed by the Procurement Cell, Provisioning Directorate, New Delhi.
The vehicles are for two BSF formations: Ftr BSF Jammu (delivery at PIN 181124) and Ftr BSF Kashmir (delivery at PIN 190021 in the Budgam area of J&K). The split between the two formations is not indicated in the tender summary provided. Procurement will be on an open two cover basis. The first cover will be for the fee, pre-qualification and technical documents and the second cover will be for the financial bid. The tender requires an earnest money deposit (EMD) of Rs 47.95 lakh to be paid offline to the Drawing and Disbursing Officer, BSF Headquarters, New Delhi. The information supplied also contains exemptions for eligible bidders (M/SMEs and Startups).
Pre-bid meeting: 21st October at 11 am in the Conference Hall on the 1st floor of Block 10, Force HQ BSF, CGO Complex, Lodhi Road, New Delhi. Clarification window closes on 22nd October at 4 pm. Bids to be submitted by 3 pm on 2nd November and will be opened at 4 pm on 3rd November.
The tender’s full technical specification (including the required protection level, seating capacity and mobility requirements) is in the procurement documents. That will dictate what type of vehicle the manufacturers have to supply and to what extent the existing platforms will be able to meet the BSF’s requirements. The summary available doesn’t identify a preferred vehicle or a potential supplier.
A useful point of reference is provided by a separate procurement exercise undertaken by the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF). In 2025 the CRPF reportedly placed an order with Mahindra Defence Systems for 642 Light Bullet Proof Vehicles in combat configuration at a total cost of around ₹325.7 crore (approximately ₹50.74 lakh per vehicle). That’s a useful benchmark but it cannot be taken as the price we’d expect to pay for the BSF order as the quantities, specifications and the nature of the contract could be very different.

morning.title: Apple faces Indian engineer’s bias lawsuit
morning.text: Apple Inc. lost an early round in a discrimination lawsuit brought in the U.S. by a female engineer from India who says her two managers -- one from her country, the other from Pakistan -- treated her as they would in their own countries: as a subservient.The woman’s case in California state court is the latest to allege workplace bias in Silicon Valley that focuses on cultural prejudices of some tech workers from South Asia. Cisco Systems Inc. is fighting a suit brought by California’s civil rights agency alleging bias against a member of India’s so-called lower castes, known as Dalits.Anita Nariani Schulze is part of the Sindhi minority -- she is Hindu, with ancestry in the Sindh region of what is now Pakistan. Her complaint alleges that her senior and direct managers, both male, consistently excluded her from meetings while inviting her male counterparts, criticized her, micromanaged her work, and deprived her of bonuses, despite positive performance evaluations and significant team contributions.Schulze claims the managers’ animus reflects sexism, racism, religious bias and discrimination on the basis of national origin. The Sindhi Hindu nationality is “known for its technical acumen” and its gender equality, she says, which “exacerbated the managers’ discriminatory treatment.”In a tentative ruling on Wednesday, Santa Clara County Superior Court Judge Sunil R. Kulkarni rejected Apple’s request to toss out the suit. While not ruling on the merits of the case, Kulkarni said Schulze had adequately supported her legal claims. Apple had argued her claims weren’t specific enough and were based on stereotypes.But the judge rejected Schulze’s request to represent a class of female Apple employees who suffered job discrimination over the last four years. He agreed with Apple that she didn’t show a pattern of discrimination that could be applied to a broader group.It wasn’t clear from the court’s docket whether the judge will hold a hearing Thursday before issuing a final ruling.Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.In the Cisco case, the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing alleged that two Indian employees at the San Jose-based company discriminated against a Dalit co-worker on the basis of caste.Cisco has denied the claims, insisting it has “zero tolerance for discrimination.” It also said the lawsuit should be tossed out because caste isn’t a protected category under U.S. civil rights law.
